definition: Dogma means a belief or set of beliefs laid down by an authority as unquestionably true — principles to be accepted, not examined.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word dogma. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know dogma should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The magazine's dogma — never end a review with a question — outlived four editors-in-chief, though none of them could say who had made the rule.

Conviction is weaker than dogma: a conviction is firmly held, but it is still yours — argument and evidence can reach it. Dogma has been sealed by authority, and challenging it is treated as betrayal rather than debate.
Taboo goes further than dogma: dogma forbids doubting the belief, while a taboo forbids even raising the subject — the question itself becomes unspeakable.

Doctrine is the neutral word for a body of teachings — a church, party, or school can state its doctrine and happily debate it. Dogma is doctrine with the door closed: laid down as beyond question, so that doubt itself becomes the offense.

Orthodoxy is whatever opinion a community currently treats as the approved, correct one — the pressure to conform comes sideways, from the group. Dogma comes down from authority as fixed truth; you can quietly drift from orthodoxy, but dogma is enforced.

For decades the studio ran on dogma: animation is for children, a musical needs a villain, sixty minutes is the ceiling.
Nobody could say where the rules came from, only that questioning them in a pitch meeting ended careers — until one film broke all three and became the studio's biggest hit.
That is the mark of dogma: the beliefs sit above argument.
Evidence is never offered because none is thought needed — the authority of the rule is the whole case, and a doubter is treated as disloyal rather than curious.
Dogma is almost always an accusation now: call a belief dogma and you are saying it survives on authority instead of evidence.
Doctrine and creed can be neutral self-descriptions; orthodoxy names the group's approved line; dogma is the hard case — fixed, enforced, and closed.
Science keeps one famous exception, the 'central dogma' of molecular biology, a deliberately wry name for a rule that did, in the end, get revised.

For most of a century, medical dogma held that stomach ulcers came from stress and spicy food.
It was not offered as a hypothesis; it was taught as settled fact, and researchers who suggested an infection might be to blame struggled to get a hearing.
Journals returned their papers, and conference panels waved the question away.
When two Australian scientists finally proved a bacterium was the culprit, the discovery was resisted for years before it was celebrated.
The episode is now taught to first-year students as a warning: a belief becomes dangerous the moment questioning it does.
